prompt: What would you do if a developer told you that a bug you reported was working as designed, and you disagreed?
variants: How would you handle a bug that the developer rejects?
intent: Checks whether you resolve it with evidence and the written requirement rather than ego.
answerGuide: Re-check the requirement or acceptance criteria and the exact steps first.
Ask the developer to walk you through their intent; you may learn something.
If the gap is real, bring user impact and evidence to whoever owns the requirement for a ruling.
pitfalls: Giving up without recording the disagreement.
followUps: What if the requirement was silent on it?
Who decides when you cannot agree?
How would you record the outcome?

prompt: What would you do if two teammates asked you for conflicting things and both said theirs was urgent?
variants: How do you respond when two people each claim top priority?
intent: Looks for transparency instead of silently choosing.
answerGuide: Get both requests in one place, with deadlines and impact.
Tell both people about the conflict and ask them, or the common manager, to decide.
Confirm the decision in writing.
pitfalls: Picking whoever is more senior without discussion.
Trying to do both and failing.
followUps: What if the manager is unavailable?
How would you decide yourself if you had to?
How do you keep both people informed?

prompt: What would you do if a coworker kept taking credit for your work?
variants: How would you handle someone presenting your work as theirs?
intent: Tests whether you can raise credit-taking directly and without hostility, with facts and a request, before going to a manager.
answerGuide: Check facts and consider whether it was one incident or a pattern.
Talk to the person privately and specifically first.
Make your work visible going forward (written updates), and involve your manager if it persists.
followUps: What exactly would you say?
What if they denied it?
How would you make your work visible?

prompt: What would you do if a customer became angry and started shouting or writing hostile messages?
variants: How do you respond to an abusive customer?
intent: Checks de-escalation: acknowledge, stay calm, set a boundary on abuse, and solve the actual problem or escalate.
answerGuide: Stay calm, acknowledge the frustration, and restate the problem.
Move to what you can do next with a specific timeline.
Set a boundary if abuse continues and escalate by policy.
followUps: What words do you use first?
When do you end the conversation?
Who do you tell afterwards?

prompt: What would you do if you started the day with five tickets and a manager message that a new urgent one just came in?
variants: How would you handle a new urgent request on top of a full queue?
intent: Tests a triage rule for a morning of competing work plus the message that tells the manager what moves.
answerGuide: Check severity and who is affected rather than trusting the word 'urgent'.
Decide what shifts and tell the owners of the delayed items.
Confirm the plan with your manager if the trade-off is unclear.
pitfalls: Treating every flag as top priority.
followUps: What makes something truly urgent?
What do you tell the delayed requester?
What if it is not really urgent?

prompt: What would you do if the backlog had far more items than the team could finish and every stakeholder wanted theirs first?
variants: How would you handle an overloaded backlog with competing stakeholders?
intent: Checks how you rank an overloaded backlog with stated criteria and handle stakeholders who lose out.
answerGuide: Agree on criteria (customer impact, risk, effort, dependencies) and apply them openly.
Show stakeholders the ranking and trade-offs.
Document what is deferred and review it regularly.
followUps: What framework might you use?
What if a senior person disagrees?
How do you keep deferred items visible?

prompt: What would you do if you had one day left before a release and ten test cases still to run?
variants: How do you decide what to test when time runs out?
intent: Tests risk-based selection of ten test cases when only part can run, and honest reporting of what was not covered.
answerGuide: Rank cases by risk: critical flows, recent changes, areas with past defects.
Run the highest-risk first and note what is untested.
Report the coverage gap clearly so the release decision is informed.
followUps: Who decides to release with gaps?
What would you call out explicitly?
How could you avoid this next time?

prompt: What would you do if your manager and a stakeholder gave you different priorities?
variants: Who do you listen to if two leaders disagree on your priorities?
intent: Checks that you surface a conflict between a manager and a stakeholder rather than choosing silently or obeying the louder one.
answerGuide: Do not choose silently; clarify with your manager.
Bring facts about the conflict and trade-offs.
Follow the decision and update the stakeholder.
followUps: What if your manager says to follow the stakeholder?
How would you tell the stakeholder?
What if it keeps happening?

prompt: What would you do if you realized you had made an error in a report that was already sent to a customer or leadership?
variants: How would you handle finding your own mistake after sending something?
intent: Tests speed and honesty in correcting a sent report: tell the recipient, give the right figure and say how it happened.
answerGuide: Confirm the error and its impact quickly.
Tell your manager and the recipients right away with a corrected version.
Add a check to prevent a repeat.
followUps: Who would you tell first?
How would you phrase the correction?
What check would you add?

prompt: What would you do if you saw that a project you were on was heading toward failure?
variants: How do you respond when a project is going off the rails?
intent: Looks for early, factual warning to the right people when a project is failing, with options, instead of waiting for it to collapse.
answerGuide: Identify the specific risks with evidence.
Raise them early with options.
Help re-plan and track the new plan.
pitfalls: Waiting for someone else to notice.
followUps: Who would you tell?
What options would you offer?
What if leadership disagreed?

prompt: What would you do if you finished your work early and nobody gave you anything new?
variants: What do you do with spare time at work?
intent: Checks what you do with spare time: ask for work, help the team, improve a process or learn, without waiting to be told.
answerGuide: Ask your manager or team if anyone needs help first.
Look for backlog cleanup, documentation or process gaps.
Check that the self-started work is useful and agreed on.
followUps: What would you pick first?
How would you check it was valuable?
How would you tell your manager?

prompt: What would you do if you noticed a recurring complaint in tickets that nobody was tracking?
variants: How would you handle spotting a pattern in feedback?
intent: Tests whether you notice a pattern in tickets, quantify it and route it to someone who can fix the root cause.
answerGuide: Quantify it: count, trend, affected users.
Write a concise summary with a suggested action.
Share it with the owner and follow up.
pitfalls: Proposing a big solution without data.
followUps: How would you count it?
Who is the owner?
What if they say it is low priority?

prompt: What would you do if a request landed in your queue that clearly belonged to another team?
variants: How do you handle tickets that are not yours?
intent: Checks that you get a misrouted request to the right team with context and follow up, instead of dropping or hoarding it.
answerGuide: Do not bounce it silently; route it with context to the right team.
Tell the requester what is happening and when to expect a response.
Follow up that the other team received it.
followUps: What context would you add?
How do you follow up?
What if the other team ignores it?

prompt: What would you do if you had to explain a delay to a customer who was counting on a feature?
variants: How would you tell a customer a promised feature will be late?
intent: Tests structure for bad news: say the delay first, the reason plainly, the new date, and what you offer meanwhile.
answerGuide: Contact them early, before the date passes.
Give the reason briefly, the new estimate and any interim option.
Set the next update date and keep it.
followUps: What if they threaten to leave?
How sure should the new date be?
What interim option could you offer?

prompt: What would you do if you sent an email or message and got no response on something time sensitive?
variants: How do you follow up on unanswered requests?
intent: Checks how you chase a time-sensitive message: a second channel, a specific ask and a sensible escalation point.
answerGuide: Check that the message was clear and sent to the right person.
Follow up on a different channel with a short, specific ask.
Escalate to an alternate contact or manager with context if the deadline is at risk.
followUps: How long would you wait?
What would the follow-up say?
Who is the escalation?

prompt: What would you do if you realized in a meeting that people were using the same word to mean different things?
variants: How would you handle a misunderstanding about terms or requirements in a meeting?
intent: Looks for the BA instinct to stop a meeting and define a term when people use one word for different things.
answerGuide: Pause and restate each definition.
Agree on a shared term, ideally with an example.
Record it in the notes or glossary.
followUps: How would you interrupt politely?
Where would you record it?
What if senior people disagree?

prompt: What would you do if a stakeholder asked for a big change late in the sprint or project?
variants: How do you handle a late scope change request?
intent: Tests change control with diplomacy when a stakeholder wants a large late change: impact, options and a decision by the owner.
answerGuide: Understand the real need and urgency.
Assess impact on scope, time and quality, and present options.
Get the decision from the right owner and record it.
followUps: What options would you present?
Who approves?
What if it is a senior executive?

prompt: What would you do if a stakeholder kept changing their mind about requirements?
variants: How do you work with someone who cannot decide?
intent: Checks how you give structure to a stakeholder who keeps changing requirements: written versions, sign-off points and visible cost.
answerGuide: Understand why: unclear goal, new information, or pressure above them.
Anchor on the goal and use examples or prototypes to make decisions concrete.
Log decisions and changes with dates and get sign-off.
followUps: What would you ask?
How would you limit the cost?
How would you document it?

prompt: What would you do if a stakeholder did not attend meetings or respond to requests, but their input was required?
variants: How do you get input from an unresponsive stakeholder?
intent: Tests persistence and workaround planning for an absent stakeholder whose input is needed, including escalation.
answerGuide: Learn their preferred channel and make requests small and specific.
Offer a default decision with a deadline.
Escalate through the sponsor if blocked.
pitfalls: Deciding for them without telling anyone.
followUps: What is a default with a deadline?
When do you escalate?
How do you keep the project moving?

prompt: What would you do if a customer reported a problem you could not reproduce?
variants: How do you handle an issue that works fine on your side?
intent: Methodical investigation and customer empathy.
answerGuide: Ask for exact steps, environment, time, and screenshots or logs.
Try matching their conditions.
Keep them informed and escalate with evidence if still unresolved.
pitfalls: Telling them it works for you.
followUps: What do you ask them first?
What do you attach to an escalation?
What if they are impatient?

prompt: What would you do if a customer asked for a feature your product did not have?
variants: How do you respond to a feature request?
intent: Honest expectation setting and feedback routing.
answerGuide: Understand the problem behind the request.
Offer a workaround if one exists without promising a date.
Log the request with context and tell the customer what happens next.
pitfalls: Logging a request without the use case.
followUps: What do you capture in the request?
How do you avoid overpromising?
How do you close the loop?

prompt: What would you do if a customer threatened to cancel because of a problem?
variants: How do you handle a customer at risk of leaving?
intent: Checks retention thinking: find the real problem behind a cancellation threat, bring in help and propose a concrete plan.
answerGuide: Listen to the cause and acknowledge the impact.
Involve the right internal owners and commit to a clear plan.
Follow up until it is resolved and check satisfaction.
pitfalls: Dropping the account after the fix.
followUps: Who do you loop in?
What would you promise?
How would you follow up?

prompt: What would you do if a customer's issue was caused by their own mistake?
variants: How do you tell a customer the problem was on their side?
intent: Tests how you fix a customer's self-inflicted problem without blame and notice if the product made the mistake easy.
answerGuide: Solve the problem first.
Explain the cause neutrally and how to avoid it.
Consider whether the product or documentation made the mistake easy.
followUps: How would you word it?
How would you feed it back?
What if they got defensive?

prompt: What would you do if an application suddenly stopped working for several users?
variants: How would you troubleshoot an outage report?
intent: Checks a troubleshooting order for a sudden multi-user failure: scope, recent changes, evidence, escalation, communication.
answerGuide: Confirm scope: who, since when, what changed.
Check for known incidents, recent releases and logs.
Communicate status, escalate with evidence, and document the resolution.
followUps: What do you check first?
When do you escalate?
What do you tell users?

prompt: What would you do if you were assigned a task you did not know how to start?
variants: How do you start something unfamiliar?
intent: Tests how you start a task you do not know: break it down, find examples and people, ask a specific question early.
answerGuide: Clarify the goal and what done looks like.
Look for existing examples, documentation or people who did it before.
Break it into small steps and share an early draft.
followUps: Who would you ask?
How early would you share a draft?
How do you know when you are stuck?

prompt: What would you do if a metric you track suddenly dropped by thirty percent?
variants: How would you investigate a sudden change in a KPI?
intent: Tests analytic triage for a 30 percent metric drop: check data validity first, then segments, then events.
answerGuide: First check data quality and definition changes.
Segment by time, product area, customer, and compare to recent changes.
Form hypotheses, test them, and report findings with confidence level.
followUps: What would you check first?
How would you segment?
Who would you tell, and when?

prompt: What would you do if you found a small inconsistency in a document everyone had already approved?
variants: How would you handle spotting an error after sign-off?
intent: Checks whether you will speak up about a small error in an approved document and how you raise it without drama.
answerGuide: Verify it is a real inconsistency.
Raise it quickly to the author with the exact location and suggestion.
Assess impact and track the correction.
pitfalls: Staying silent because it was approved.
followUps: How would you word it?
What if it were large?
What if the author disagreed?

prompt: What would you do in your first 30 days in a new role in a domain you did not know?
variants: How would you ramp up in your first month?
intent: Looks for a concrete 30-day plan for an unfamiliar domain: users, vocabulary, documents, shadowing, first small deliverable.
answerGuide: Learn the product, users and vocabulary first.
Meet your team and stakeholders and learn how work flows.
Pick a small deliverable early and ask for feedback.
followUps: Who would you meet first?
What would be your first deliverable?
How would you know you were on track?

prompt: What would you do if your team switched to a tool you had never used?
variants: How do you adopt a new system quickly?
intent: Checks how you get productive on an unfamiliar tool: map it to known tools, use sandboxes and documentation, practise on low-risk work.
answerGuide: Map it to tools you know.
Use documentation, a sandbox and a colleague for questions.
Practice on real but low-risk work.
followUps: How would you practice safely?
Who would you ask?
How do you tell when you are proficient?

prompt: What would you do if your manager changed the project direction after you had done a lot of work?
variants: How do you handle wasted effort after a pivot?
intent: Tests professionalism when direction changes after your work: understand why, salvage what you can, re-plan without resentment.
answerGuide: Understand the reason for the change.
Identify what is reusable.
Move on without resentment and adjust the plan.
followUps: What would you ask your manager?
What can be reused?
How do you stay motivated?

prompt: What would you do if a teammate was not carrying their share of a group project?
variants: How do you handle an underperforming colleague?
intent: Checks a fair approach to a teammate not pulling their weight: ask first, then clear expectations, then the manager.
answerGuide: Check whether there is a reason, such as unclear expectations or personal issues.
Talk to them privately and offer help.
Involve the lead only if the problem persists.
followUps: What would you say?
When would you tell the manager?
What if they were senior?

prompt: What would you do if you noticed a colleague was struggling or overwhelmed?
variants: How do you respond to a stressed teammate?
intent: Tests kind, specific support for an overwhelmed colleague and knowing when to point them to their manager.
answerGuide: Check in privately and kindly.
Offer specific help.
Suggest they raise it with their manager if workload is the cause.
followUps: What would you offer?
What if they said they were fine?
When would you tell the manager?

prompt: What would you do if a meeting was running off topic and nobody else was stepping in?
variants: How would you bring a meeting back on track?
intent: Looks for gentle facilitation when a meeting drifts: restate the goal, park topics and agree actions.
answerGuide: Restate the goal and time left.
Park off-topic items in a list.
Confirm decisions and actions at the end.
followUps: What words would you use?
What if a senior person drove the tangent?
Where do the parked items go?

prompt: What would you do if a production issue hit during your shift and you were the only person available?
variants: How would you handle an urgent incident alone?
intent: Checks composure when alone on a production issue: follow the runbook, scope impact, escalate, and communicate.
answerGuide: Assess severity and who is affected.
Follow the documented procedure and escalate to the on-call owner.
Keep stakeholders updated and write down the timeline.
followUps: What would you do first?
What if nobody answered the escalation?
What would you document?

prompt: What would you do if your manager asked you to take on a rush task while you were already at capacity?
variants: How do you respond to extra work when overloaded?
intent: Tests an honest capacity conversation: show the current load and ask which item should move, rather than silently accepting.
answerGuide: Say yes to the goal but show your current load.
Ask what should be moved or delayed.
Agree on the plan and timeline.
followUps: What would you say?
What if everything is critical?
How would you track it?

prompt: What would you do if the acceptance criteria on a ticket were missing or unclear when you started testing?
variants: How do you test a feature with no clear requirements?
intent: Checks how you test against missing acceptance criteria: ask the author, write down assumptions and confirm them before executing.
answerGuide: Ask the author or product owner and note the answers on the ticket.
Use related tickets, documentation and similar features to infer behavior.
Test on stated assumptions and flag them in your report.
followUps: Who would you ask?
How would you record assumptions?
What if nobody could answer?

prompt: What would you do if you were handed a project with no documentation and the previous owner had left?
variants: How do you take over an undocumented process?
intent: Tests discovery on an undocumented inheritance: find people and artefacts, map what exists, write it down.
answerGuide: Collect artifacts: tickets, emails, system settings.
Interview users and stakeholders.
Write down what you learn so the next person is not stuck.
followUps: Where would you look first?
Who would you interview?
How do you verify your understanding?

prompt: What would you do if you noticed a process that wasted a lot of time but everyone said it had always been done that way?
variants: How would you suggest improving a long-standing process?
intent: Checks change leadership: learn why the process exists, measure the waste, pilot with the people affected.
answerGuide: Learn why it exists first.
Measure the waste to build a case.
Pilot a small change with the people involved.
followUps: How would you measure it?
Who would you involve first?
What if someone said no?

prompt: What would you do if you found a serious bug the day before a major release?
variants: How do you handle a late-found critical defect?
intent: Tests release judgement for a serious day-before bug: evidence, options and a decision by the owner.
answerGuide: Confirm and document it with steps, impact and scope.
Tell the product owner and team immediately.
Present options (fix, delay, ship with workaround) and let the owner decide.
pitfalls: Deciding to block the release alone.
followUps: What would you include in the report?
Who decides to ship?
What if they ship anyway?

prompt: What would you do if you were told to skip testing to meet a deadline?
variants: How would you respond to pressure to ship untested work?
intent: Checks integrity when told to skip testing: state the risk, offer a minimum test set, and record the decision.
answerGuide: Explain risk in business terms.
Offer reduced scope testing targeted at highest-risk areas.
Make sure the risk acceptance is explicit and recorded.
followUps: What minimum would you propose?
Who accepts the risk?
How do you record it?

prompt: What would you do if two reports gave different numbers for the same metric?
variants: How do you reconcile conflicting data?
intent: Tests reconciliation logic for two reports with different numbers: compare definitions, filters and timing before blaming data.
answerGuide: Check definitions, filters, time ranges and data sources.
Trace to the source records for a sample.
Document the correct definition and tell users which to trust.
followUps: What do you check first?
How do you decide which is right?
How do you prevent it?

prompt: What would you do if a stakeholder asked you for a number you were not confident about?
variants: How do you handle sharing uncertain data?
intent: Checks honesty about confidence when asked for a number you cannot stand behind: caveat it and give a date for the firm figure.
answerGuide: Give the number with its caveats or a range.
Say what you would do to firm it up and by when.
Avoid presenting a guess as fact.
followUps: How would you word the caveat?
What would you check?
What if they insisted on one number?

prompt: What would you do if someone asked you for information about a customer or patient that you were not sure they were allowed to see?
variants: How do you handle requests for sensitive data?
intent: Tests privacy judgement when asked for customer or patient details: verify authority, share the minimum, and escalate if unsure.
answerGuide: Do not share until you verify identity and permission.
Follow the policy or ask a privacy or compliance contact.
Document the request and the outcome.
pitfalls: Refusing without offering the proper route.
followUps: How would you verify?
What if they were senior?
What would you document?

prompt: What would you do if you accidentally sent confidential information to the wrong person?
variants: How would you handle a data mix-up?
intent: Checks incident honesty after a misdirected confidential message: report immediately, contain and learn.
answerGuide: Report immediately to your manager or the proper security contact.
Ask the recipient to delete it if appropriate and record the incident.
Learn what check would have prevented it.
followUps: Who would you tell first?
What would you document?
What would you change?

prompt: What would you do if you received feedback you thought was unfair?
variants: How do you handle criticism you disagree with?
intent: Tests composure with unfair-feeling feedback: ask for specifics, check for truth in it and respond after reflecting.
answerGuide: Listen without arguing and ask for examples.
Reflect before responding; look for a true part.
Discuss calmly if you still disagree.
followUps: What would you ask?
When would you push back?
How do you decide if it is fair?

prompt: What would you do if a meeting-heavy week left you little time for your own work?
variants: How do you protect focus time?
intent: Checks how you protect focus time in a meeting-heavy week: decline or shorten meetings, block time, renegotiate priorities.
answerGuide: Review which meetings need you.
Block focus time and decline or shorten low-value meetings.
Talk to your manager about the load.
followUps: How do you decide which to skip?
What do you tell organizers?
What if your manager insists?

prompt: What would you do if you were blocked and your remote team was in different time zones for the next several hours?
variants: How do you stay productive when waiting on teammates asynchronously?
intent: Tests async unblocking across time zones: complete messages, parallel work and clear check-back times.
answerGuide: Write a clear, complete question with what you tried.
Switch to other useful work while waiting.
Use shared docs and ticket comments so the answer waits for them rather than a meeting.
followUps: What does a good async question contain?
What would you work on meanwhile?
What if it was urgent?

prompt: What would you do if your internet or computer failed during an important workday?
variants: What is your backup plan for remote work problems?
intent: Checks remote contingency: backup connection or device, telling the team at once and which work can continue.
answerGuide: Describe a real backup: mobile hotspot, secondary location, spare device options.
Notify your manager immediately.
Share how you keep work accessible in the cloud.
followUps: What backup do you have?
Who would you notify and how?
What would you miss?

prompt: What would you do on a call or chat when you had no idea what the answer to a customer's question was?
variants: How do you handle a question you cannot answer?
intent: Tests honesty when you do not know the answer on a live contact: say so, find the answer, and commit to a follow-up time.
answerGuide: Say you will find out, not guess.
Use the knowledge base or ask a colleague while keeping the customer informed.
Follow up with the answer and add it to documentation.
pitfalls: Promising a callback you do not keep.
followUps: What would you say?
How long do you keep them waiting?
How do you capture the answer?

prompt: What would you do if a training session or onboarding with a new customer went badly and users seemed lost?
variants: How would you recover a failing onboarding call?
intent: Tests adapting a training session that is not landing: check understanding, change the format, simplify.
answerGuide: Pause and ask what is confusing.
Simplify to the one task they need most.
Follow up with a short guide and a check-in.
followUps: What would you ask them?
How would you restructure?
What would the follow-up include?

prompt: Your release goes out tomorrow and UAT turns up a critical bug in shift cancellation. The product owner wants to ship anyway. What do you do?
variants: A critical bug appears the day before release. Walk me through your decisions.
intent: Tests whether you protect users with evidence and options rather than a veto or silence: impact, workaround, fix time and a decision owner.
answerGuide: Reproduce and document the bug with steps, scope and impact (who is affected, data at risk, workaround).
Give the owner clear options: fix and delay, ship with a mitigation, or ship with the feature disabled, with the risk of each.
Let the person who owns the decision decide and record it; confirm you will retest any hotfix.
Prepare support notes if it ships.
pitfalls: Refusing to release as if you owned the decision.
followUps: What if the owner still says ship and you disagree?
What would make it a true blocker?
How do you retest a rushed fix?

prompt: A developer closes your bug as 'works as designed', but you think users will be confused. What next?
variants: How do you handle disagreement with a developer about a defect?
intent: Checks that you separate defect from requirement gap and can argue from user impact without a power struggle.
answerGuide: Check the requirement or story: is the design documented, and does the behaviour match it?
If it does, reframe as a usability or requirement issue with evidence of user impact and send it to the owner.
Talk to the developer to understand their reasoning before escalating.
Accept the decision once made and note it.
pitfalls: Dropping it without telling the owner.
followUps: How would you show user impact?
What if the documentation is silent?
Have you changed your mind after such a talk?

prompt: At the end of UAT, the customer's manager says she will not sign off because she dislikes how one screen looks, though all test scenarios passed. What do you do?
variants: The customer won't sign off after UAT passed. How do you proceed?
intent: Separates acceptance criteria from preference and checks your ability to turn a stuck sign-off into a concrete decision.
answerGuide: Ask what specifically concerns her and which business need it affects.
Compare with the agreed criteria: if met, say so kindly and show the evidence.
Classify the feedback as a defect, a change request or a preference, and offer a plan for each (fix now, add to backlog, decline).
Agree a date for sign-off and escalate to the sponsor if the loop continues.
followUps: What if she has a point?
How would you avoid this next time?
Who can overrule her?

prompt: Half your test cases are written when the product owner changes the requirement. What do you do?
variants: Requirements change after you have prepared tests. How do you cope?
intent: Tests practical test maintenance: assess impact, update only what matters, and keep traceability.
answerGuide: Get the change in writing and read it against your cases to list the affected ones.
Update or retire those, add new cases for the new behaviour, and keep the links to the story current.
Tell the team the test effort impact so the plan stays honest.
Raise the pattern in retrospective if changes come late repeatedly.
pitfalls: Leaving obsolete cases in the suite.
followUps: How do you estimate the extra test time?
Would you test the old behaviour?
How do you reduce rework from late changes?

prompt: The test environment is down on the day UAT starts. What do you do?
variants: Your test environment fails right before UAT. What now?
intent: Probes communication and recovery: protect users' time, find the owner, and adjust the plan.
answerGuide: Check scope: who owns the environment, what is the cause, and an estimated fix time.
Tell the UAT participants quickly with a new start or an interim plan, so you do not waste their limited time.
Use the downtime for preparation: data checks, scripts, training.
After recovery, run a quick smoke check before restarting and capture the lesson.
pitfalls: Letting users show up to a broken environment.
Switching to production to save time.
followUps: Would you ever use production?
What if the outage lasts days?
How would you prevent a repeat?

prompt: You are handed a feature to test with no written requirements and the developer has left. How do you start?
variants: How do you test something nobody documented?
intent: Tests discovery skills: who knows the behaviour, what evidence exists, and how you write down what you assume.
answerGuide: Gather evidence: similar existing features, tickets, the code history if available, users and support who know it.
Write the assumed behaviours as a short list and have an owner confirm or correct them.
Test with exploratory sessions around that list and log questions separately from defects.
Document what you learned for the next person.
pitfalls: Testing against your own assumptions only.
followUps: Who would you ask first?
How do you decide expected results?
How do you record findings?

prompt: The pipeline's automated tests turn red an hour before the release cut. Two failures look unrelated to the change. What do you do?
variants: Automated checks fail late in the release. How do you decide to proceed?
intent: Tests judgement about trust in automated tests and a disciplined way to separate real regressions from noise.
answerGuide: Read the failures: error text, screenshots, and whether the same tests failed on the previous run.
Rerun once to check for flakiness; manually verify the covered flows if time allows.
Report the facts to the release owner: real regression, environment problem or flaky test, with confidence.
Create tickets for the failing tests; do not mute them silently.
pitfalls: Ignoring red because it is probably flaky.
followUps: How do you manually verify quickly?
What if one failure is real?
How would you reduce this problem?

prompt: Four days into a two-week sprint the customer's director asks for a different approach to the notification feature. What do you do?
variants: A stakeholder changes requirements in the middle of a sprint.
intent: Tests protecting sprint commitments while responding to real business needs: impact analysis and a decision, not a reflex yes or no.
answerGuide: Understand the reason and urgency: what has changed in the business.
Assess the effect on the sprint goal: work done, work wasted, time needed, risks.
Offer options: finish the sprint as planned and prioritise the change next, swap scope with equal effort, or stop the sprint only if the goal is now meaningless.
The product owner decides; update stories and tell the team and testers.
followUps: What if they say it's critical?
How do you record the change?
How do you tell the developers?

prompt: A developer says your requirement is too expensive, and the stakeholder insists on it. How do you get to a decision?
variants: The business wants it, engineering says no. What do you do?
intent: Checks that you translate between sides and bring options with costs rather than relaying a fight.
answerGuide: Ask the developer what drives the cost and which parts are expensive.
Ask the stakeholder what outcome they need; propose cheaper alternatives such as a simpler version or phased approach.
Present the options with effort, risk and value to both and let the owner choose.
Document the decision and rationale.
pitfalls: Telling each side what they want to hear.
followUps: What if the cheaper option fails the need?
How do you estimate value?
What if both stay stuck?

prompt: A stakeholder says, 'Add a column to the report that shows X.' You suspect the real problem is different. What do you do?
variants: Someone asks for a specific change that may not solve their problem.
intent: Checks the BA instinct of finding the need behind the request without being obstructive.
answerGuide: Ask what they will do with the column and what decision it supports.
Confirm the underlying problem and success measure, and check whether the column answers it.
If yes, do it; if there is a better way, show a quick mock-up or option.
Capture the problem statement in the ticket and not just the requested change.
followUps: How do you ask 'why' without annoying them?
What if they insist?
How do you record the need?

prompt: The largest customer wants feature A this quarter. Internally the team believes feature B helps all customers more. How do you advise?
variants: Customer demand conflicts with the team's view of value.
intent: Tests structured trade-off reasoning that uses evidence rather than loudness.
answerGuide: Gather evidence for both: number of customers and revenue affected, effort, strategic fit and risks of ignoring the large customer.
Look for a split: a minimum version of A, or a workaround, plus B on schedule.
Present a recommendation with the trade-off to the decision owner.
Communicate the result to the customer honestly.
pitfalls: Choosing the biggest customer by default.
followUps: What if you have little data?
What if the customer escalates?
How would you word the answer to them?

prompt: The operations director tells you to focus on the export bug; the head of customer success says the onboarding checklist is more urgent. Both outrank you. What do you do?
variants: Two managers give you conflicting priorities.
intent: A classic stress test for coordination roles: surface the conflict, give information, and let the right person decide.
answerGuide: Do not pick quietly. Get both items' facts: impact, deadline, effort, who is blocked.
Put the conflict in front of both managers (or their shared manager) in one short message with a recommendation and the cost of each choice.
Continue the work that is clearly valuable while waiting for a decision, and keep the log of what you were told.
Communicate the decision to both once made.
pitfalls: Telling each manager what they want to hear.
followUps: What if they will not talk to each other?
What if you have to decide within the hour?
How do you prevent this in future?

prompt: It is day eight of a ten-day sprint and a key story is only half done. What do you do?
variants: A sprint story will not be done by the end. What now?
intent: Tests honest early signalling and options: reduce scope, ask for help, or move the story, not hide the slip.
answerGuide: Raise it now at standup, not at the review.
Ask the team what remains and what is truly needed to meet the sprint goal; consider cutting scope to a usable slice.
Check whether swarming or removing a blocker would finish it, and whether testing can start in parallel.
If it will not finish, move it with a clear reason, inform stakeholders, and discuss the root cause at retrospective.
followUps: Would you extend the sprint?
How would you tell the stakeholder?
What would you change in planning?

prompt: A feature the team shipped six weeks ago is used by only 8 percent of customers. What do you do?
variants: Nobody uses the feature you shipped. How do you respond?
intent: Tests outcome orientation: checking usage and talking to users before blaming or defending the feature.
answerGuide: Define what adoption you expected and why; check the data quality and who could use it.
Investigate the funnel: awareness, access, understanding, repeat use; talk to a few users and non-users.
Fix the cheapest cause first (visibility, documentation, onboarding prompts), then decide whether to improve, keep, or remove the feature.
Share the learning with the team and stakeholders honestly.
pitfalls: Adding more features without checking why.
followUps: What would you ask non-users?
What if the feature is wrong?
How long do you wait before judging?

prompt: Engineering says a library has a security notice that needs a week of work. A customer wants a promised report in the same week. How do you decide?
variants: Security fix versus customer-visible commitment.
intent: Checks risk-based prioritisation and willingness to renegotiate a commitment with facts.
answerGuide: Get the facts on severity and exploitability from engineering and what the promise is worth to the customer.
If the risk is real, make the security work the priority; if it is low, schedule it with a date.
Talk to the customer early with a new date or a partial deliverable.
Record the decision and rationale.
pitfalls: Dropping the customer commitment without a conversation.
followUps: Who decides severity?
What if you can do both with overtime?
How do you tell the customer?

prompt: The only developer who knows the notification service is out sick for the week before a committed date. What do you do?
variants: A key team member is unavailable at a critical moment.
intent: Tests contingency planning and honest communication with options instead of waiting.
answerGuide: Assess what is critical for the date and which tasks need that person.
Find cover: pair someone, use documentation, ask the person for a short asynchronous handoff if they are able, or reduce scope.
Tell the stakeholders the risk and options early, with a revised estimate and what you need from them.
Record the knowledge gap as a risk for after the release.
followUps: What if no one else can do it?
What would you cut?
How do you reduce key-person risk long term?

prompt: A sponsor wants a launch date that is three weeks sooner than your plan allows. What do you say?
variants: How do you handle an unrealistic deadline from a senior person?
intent: Tests how you push back with evidence and options, not an absolute no.
answerGuide: Understand what the date protects (a customer event, a contract).
Show the plan with the critical path and what must be true to hit the earlier date.
Offer choices: reduce scope, add resource if it helps, accept more risk with defined limits, or move the date.
Ask for a decision, record it, and plan around it.
followUps: What if they pick the risky option?
How do you quantify risk?
Who else needs to know?

prompt: The customer asks for 'one small extra field' for the third time this month. What do you do?
variants: How do you manage scope creep from small requests?
intent: Tests spotting the cumulative effect of small asks and turning them into a visible decision.
answerGuide: Track the requests and show the sum of effort and its effect on the date.
Offer a choice: add them with an updated date, swap for lower-priority scope, or batch them into a later release.
Reconfirm the objective so additions can be judged against it.
Keep the tone collaborative; log the decision.
pitfalls: Saying yes to each to avoid friction.
Bringing up the pattern only when overdue.
followUps: How do you measure each one?
What if the field is genuinely important?
How do you tell the team?

prompt: You need a sign-off to start the next phase, and the approver has not answered in four days. What do you do?
variants: Someone you depend on is not responding.
intent: Tests persistent professional follow-up and escalation ladder.
answerGuide: Re-send a short, specific message with the decision needed and a date, and offer a quick call.
Try another channel and check with their assistant or team to see if they are away.
Tell your manager the schedule risk, and ask whether a delegate can approve.
Record the attempts so the delay is clear.
followUps: When would you escalate?
What if they say 'fine' without reading?
How do you word the follow-up?

prompt: A customer insists that shifts disappearing from their list is a bug. You believe it is working as designed (shifts hide after filling). How do you respond?
variants: A customer says something is a bug and you think it is not.
intent: Tests calm disagreement: check the facts, explain the design clearly, and capture the usability signal.
answerGuide: Reproduce what they see with their account and confirm the design with documentation or the product owner.
Explain in terms of their goal: what happens and where to find the information they want, with a screenshot.
Acknowledge if the behaviour is confusing and record it as feedback or a request with the customer's words.
Do not say 'working as intended' and stop.
pitfalls: Agreeing it is a bug without checking.
followUps: What if you are wrong?
How would you flag the usability issue?
What if they escalate to your manager?

prompt: Forty tickets arrive in an hour, all saying the schedule page will not load. What do you do?
variants: How do you handle a sudden spike of identical tickets?
intent: Tests incident behaviour: recognise the pattern, alert engineering, communicate once, and protect the queue.
answerGuide: Recognise the pattern, confirm the impact quickly, and alert the on-call engineer or incident lead with evidence.
Post one status message (banner, status page, or macro) so customers get consistent information.
Link the tickets to one incident, avoid answering each separately, and keep sending updates at agreed times.
After resolution, follow up and review timing and communication.
pitfalls: Handling each ticket as a separate problem.
followUps: Who tells customers?
How do you keep a record?
What would you review afterwards?

prompt: A customer reports an error you cannot reproduce after an hour. What next?
variants: You can't reproduce a customer's bug. How do you proceed?
intent: Tests structured investigation: differences in data, role, browser and timing, and when to ask for evidence.
answerGuide: List what differs: account role, data state, browser, time, recent changes.
Ask the customer for a screen recording, exact steps, a time stamp and the record id.
Check logs or ask engineering with the time stamp and id.
Keep the customer informed of progress; if still unresolved, document findings and escalate rather than closing.
pitfalls: Closing the ticket as 'cannot reproduce' immediately.
followUps: How do you ask for a recording politely?
What would an intermittent bug need?
When do you escalate?

prompt: A customer's executive demands that you bump their ticket ahead of ten critical ones. What do you do?
variants: How do you handle pressure to jump the queue?
intent: Tests fairness and escalation: use the priority framework, listen to impact, and involve the right owner.
answerGuide: Listen and ask for the business impact; compare it against the severity rules.
If it truly is higher impact, reprioritise with your lead's approval; if not, explain the process and give an honest time frame.
Offer something useful in the meantime such as a workaround.
Tell your lead about the pressure so decisions are shared.
followUps: What if your manager says to do it?
How do you tell customers with the critical tickets?
How do you explain the priority rules?

prompt: You find that a knowledge base article sent to customers last week has a wrong step that may have affected data. What do you do?
variants: You discover your documentation caused customers harm.
intent: Combines ownership, speed and customer communication when the error is yours or your team's.
answerGuide: Correct the article immediately and note the change date.
Find who followed it using article views, tickets and replies, and the effect on their data.
Contact affected customers with a plain explanation and the fix steps.
Add a review step for steps that touch data.
followUps: How do you find affected customers?
Who approves the outreach?
How do you prevent a repeat?

prompt: The customer promised their staff data by Friday for a Monday training and has sent nothing. What do you do?
variants: The customer is late with something you depend on.
intent: Tests handling customer dependencies with firmness and options.
answerGuide: Contact the customer's lead today, state the impact plainly, and ask for a date or what is blocking them.
Offer help: a simpler template or a partial file to start with a pilot group.
Adjust the plan and tell your team, then give the customer the new dates in writing.
Escalate to the sponsor if there is no response by an agreed time.
followUps: What if it keeps happening?
How do you keep the relationship intact?
When do you change the go-live?

prompt: On go-live morning, a customer's first users report they cannot see their shifts. What do you do?
variants: Something breaks on launch day. How do you respond?
intent: Tests calm triage and communication in the highest-visibility moment of the role.
answerGuide: Gather facts: how many users, which role or location, and whether a recent change explains it; check permissions and assignments first.
Tell the customer you are on it with a next update time; get engineering help with the evidence if it is not configuration.
Offer a workaround if there is one and decide with the customer whether to continue or pause the launch.
Review the cause afterwards and update the go-live checklist.
pitfalls: Making changes in production with no record.
followUps: What would make you roll back?
Who decides?
What would you add to the checklist?

prompt: A month after go-live, only half the customer's managers use the software. What do you do?
variants: Adoption is low after launch.
intent: Tests diagnosing adoption problems before reacting.
answerGuide: Look at usage by role and location to find who is using it and who is not.
Ask non-users why: training, no time, no perceived value, access problems, or the old process being easier.
Fix the cause: refresher sessions, shorter guides, manager sponsorship, or configuration changes.
Agree an adoption target with the sponsor and track it.
followUps: Who could help you push adoption?
What if the old process is mandated?
How do you measure success?

prompt: Midway through an implementation your main contact at the customer resigns. What do you do?
variants: Your customer champion leaves during the project.
intent: Tests relationship resilience and risk management.
answerGuide: Express support, ask who takes over and when, and request a handoff meeting.
Use the written decisions and requirements to bring the new contact up to speed fast.
Reconfirm goals, dates and responsibilities; find a second sponsor.
Flag the schedule risk internally.
pitfalls: Contacting people outside the agreed channels.
followUps: How do you avoid single-contact risk?
What if the replacement disagrees with decisions?
How would you document it?

prompt: Your weekly cancellation count differs from what finance reports. A leader asks which is right. What do you say?
variants: Two reports give different numbers. Which one is correct?
intent: Tests honest reconciliation under pressure: you do not choose before you understand the difference.
answerGuide: Say you will find the cause, not guess; ask for finance's definition and time range.
Compare the definitions and run both against the same source to find the rows that differ.
Report the cause and a recommendation (agreed definition, labelled both) with your confidence.
Add a regular reconciliation check.
pitfalls: Saying both are right without explanation.
followUps: What if it's a data error in the source?
How long would you take?
Who should own the definition?

prompt: While documenting a manual process, you find that a step has been done wrongly for months. What do you do?
variants: You discover a long-running error in a process.
intent: Tests candour and impact assessment when the error is not yours.
answerGuide: Verify the issue with evidence and size the impact: records affected and consequences.
Tell the process owner right away, privately and factually.
Propose containment (stop the wrong step), correction of past records, and a fix to prevent recurrence.
Document the change in the procedure.
pitfalls: Blaming the person who did it.
followUps: How do you handle those who followed the old way?
Who must be told?
How do you check the fix?

prompt: You see a weekly manual report that takes four hours. Your manager says automate it but gives you no time. What do you do?
variants: How do you improve something with no allocated time?
intent: Tests making the case and sequencing improvement work around the day job.
answerGuide: Measure the cost: four hours a week is about 200 hours a year.
Propose a small first step (a saved query and template) that cuts time quickly.
Ask for a defined slice of time and agree the success measure.
Be open about the trade-off with other work.
pitfalls: Waiting for permission to think about it.
followUps: How would you start?
What if the report changes often?
How do you test the automated version?

prompt: You find that 3 percent of rows in a key table are duplicates and a dashboard already uses them. What do you do?
variants: You find duplicated data feeding a live report.
intent: Tests careful action on live data: measure, tell owners, and fix safely.
answerGuide: Quantify the duplicates and their effect on the metrics shown.
Notify the data owner and report users with the size of the error and what is affected.
Fix through the owner's process (a staged cleanup with backup), not by deleting rows yourself.
Add a uniqueness check and note the correction in the report.
followUps: How do you find the cause?
How do you present the corrected figures?
How would you prevent this?

prompt: An executive wants a number in ten minutes and your query needs a check you cannot finish in time. What do you do?
variants: How do you balance speed and accuracy when asked for a number urgently?
intent: Tests integrity: giving a clearly labelled provisional number with a caveat, not false precision.
answerGuide: Give the number with the caveat in the same message: preliminary, based on X, not yet checked for Y.
Say when the confirmed number will come.
Run the fastest sanity check available, such as comparing with last week.
Follow up with the confirmed figure and flag any change.
followUps: What if they quote it in a meeting?
How do you phrase the caveat?
What would you do if the final number differs?

prompt: Average time to fill a shift doubled last week. Describe your first hour.
variants: A KPI moves sharply. How do you investigate?
intent: Tests investigative order: data validity first, then segmentation, then business causes.
answerGuide: Check data issues first: late loads, changed field meaning, test data, or a time-zone shift.
Segment by region, pharmacy, emergency versus planned, and request time to see where the change sits.
Check for events: outage, product release, holiday, supply of pharmacists.
Write up findings with confidence, and propose the next test.
followUps: What if only one pharmacy changed?
How do you know it's not noise?
What would you tell the director?

prompt: The daily data file has not arrived and the report is due at nine. What do you do?
variants: The input to your report is missing close to the deadline.
intent: Tests contingency thinking and communication about data freshness.
answerGuide: Check whether the file is late or failed, and contact the owner.
Decide with the report's consumers whether to send yesterday's data labelled as such, or delay.
Mark the data as-of time clearly on the report.
Follow up on prevention: an alert for missing files.
followUps: Who decides?
How do you label it?
What alert would you add?

prompt: A customer says, 'We are not getting enough value from your software.' How do you respond?
variants: A customer questions the value of the product.
intent: Tests listening, evidence and honest planning rather than defensiveness.
answerGuide: Ask what they expected and measure; listen first.
Check usage and outcomes against that goal: where value is visible and where it is missing.
Agree a short plan with specific actions and a review date, including product gaps raised internally.
Be honest where the product cannot deliver.
pitfalls: Promising what the product cannot do.
followUps: What if they are right?
How do you bring data?
What if they still want to leave?

prompt: A customer's usage has dropped and your last two emails got no reply. What do you do?
variants: How do you re-engage a silent customer?
intent: Tests creativity and persistence within async constraints.
answerGuide: Check for explanations: seasonality, staff changes, outages.
Change the approach: a shorter message with one specific, useful observation, a different contact, or a different channel.
Involve the account owner or sponsor if the champion is gone.
Set a point after which you flag the account as at risk and plan accordingly.
followUps: Who else could you contact?
What would you say?
When do you escalate internally?

prompt: A caller says she is a pharmacist's mother and wants her son's schedule because he is not answering. What do you do?
variants: Someone asks for personal information about an employee or patient.
intent: Tests confidentiality and compassion together: do not disclose, offer a safe route.
answerGuide: Do not confirm or share schedule or employment details.
Offer to pass a message to the person through proper channels and give a general contact route.
If safety is a concern, follow the organisation's emergency procedure and escalate to a supervisor.
Record the call.
pitfalls: Giving the schedule because she sounds worried.
followUps: What if she says it's an emergency?
What if you feel something is wrong?
How do you log it?

prompt: A pharmacy manager urgently asks you to assign a pharmacist whose licence verification is pending. What do you do?
variants: Policy conflicts with an urgent request.
intent: Tests whether you hold a compliance line while helping find a legitimate alternative.
answerGuide: Explain that you cannot assign without verification and say what you can do.
Speed up verification, ask a verified colleague, or offer other coverage options.
Escalate to a supervisor or compliance contact if the manager pushes; do not bypass.
Document the request and outcome.
followUps: Who can authorise an exception?
What if a patient is at risk?
How would you speed verification?

prompt: You realise you updated the wrong patient or staff record this morning. What do you do?
variants: You made a data entry error in a sensitive system.
intent: Tests immediate disclosure, containment and correction.
answerGuide: Stop, note exactly what changed in which records, and check whether anything left the system.
Tell your supervisor now and follow the correction and incident procedure.
Correct through the approved process with the audit note.
Learn the cause (similar names, screen layout) and add a check.
followUps: Why tell even if you fixed it?
What if the change was seen by others?
What check would you add?

prompt: Exercise: six tickets arrive at once: a login failure for one user, an outage affecting a region, a how-to question, a data correction request, a feature request, a complaint from a large customer about a slow report. Put them in order and say what you reply first.
variants: Triage this queue.
intent: A common support and coordinator exercise; graders check impact-based ordering and immediate holding replies.
answerGuide: First the outage (widest impact, time critical), then the login failure if it blocks work, then the large customer's complaint with a holding reply.
How-to, data correction and feature request wait, each with the right acknowledgement.
Mention linking the outage tickets, telling the lead, and giving realistic response times.
Say what extra facts would change your order.
followUps: What if the large customer's report is blocking month-end?
Who do you tell about the outage?
How do you set expectations for the rest?

prompt: Exercise: the feature promised to a customer for Friday will be a week late because of a failed test. Draft the message to the customer.
variants: Write a delay notice to a customer.
intent: Writing test for customer-facing roles: honesty, a new date with confidence, and what you are doing to help meanwhile.
answerGuide: Lead with the news and new date, then the plain reason (quality check found an issue) without internal blame.
Say what you are doing and what it means for them; offer a workaround if there is one.
State when you will confirm or update the date.
Keep to a few short paragraphs, no jargon, no excuses.
pitfalls: Burying the delay in paragraph three.
Promising the new date without confidence.
followUps: What if they are angry?
What would you add if there were a penalty clause?
How do you check the date with engineering?

prompt: You used an AI tool to summarise a long ticket thread and later find the summary invented a decision nobody made. It is already in a status email. What do you do?
variants: An AI tool caused an error in your work.
intent: Tests responsible AI use: you own the output, correct fast and set a verification habit.
answerGuide: Correct it immediately to the readers with a short factual note.
Check the other places the summary was used.
Explain that you verify AI summaries against the source before sending anything and keep AI away from confidential data.
Adopt the habit going forward.
followUps: Which tasks do you use AI for?
What data must never go into a tool?
How do you verify?

prompt: A teammate suggests pasting a customer's full ticket history into a public AI chat tool to speed up a report. What do you do?
variants: Is it ok to put customer data into an AI tool?
intent: Privacy judgement around AI: understand data classification and the approved tools.
answerGuide: Do not paste customer or patient data into tools that are not approved.
Explain risk simply: you lose control of where the data goes.
Offer alternatives: redact or use made-up examples, or an approved tool.
Raise it with your lead if the habit persists.
pitfalls: Doing it because it is faster.
followUps: What counts as sensitive?
What would you use AI for safely?
What if there is no policy?

prompt: You are blocked at 4 pm and the person who can unblock you is asleep in a time zone nine hours away. What do you do?
variants: How do you handle async blockers?
intent: Tests async self-sufficiency: write the question once, work on something else, and remove delay.
answerGuide: Write a complete message: context, what you tried, the exact question and the options you prefer.
Check documentation and a second contact first; switch to other useful work so the block costs no time.
State when you will check back and what you will assume if you hear nothing for low-risk items.
Document the answer afterwards.
followUps: What if it is an emergency?
How do you choose between channels?
How do you write a good async question?

prompt: A short message from a colleague in chat reads as rude, and you have felt tension building over a few days. What do you do?
variants: How do you deal with tone problems in text?
intent: Tests a remote-work skill: not letting text ambiguity grow into conflict.
answerGuide: Assume good intent and reread; do not reply while annoyed.
Move to a short call or voice note and ask about the message neutrally.
Agree how you will flag urgency or concerns in future.
Follow up in writing to confirm decisions.
followUps: What if it was meant that way?
When do you involve a manager?
How do you write tone-safe messages?

prompt: A company gives you a take-home exercise that they say takes two hours, but you are at four hours and not finished. What do you do?
variants: How do you handle a take-home assignment that is running long?
intent: Interview-process question: scoping, honesty about assumptions, and professional boundaries.
answerGuide: Stop at the stated time and submit the best usable version, not an unfinished everything.
State what you completed, what you would do next and your assumptions.
Prioritise what graders probably value: correctness, clear thinking and communication.
If it is clearly longer than described, say so politely.
followUps: Would you ask clarifying questions first?
What would you cut?
Would you say if it was longer?

prompt: Live case: a software team's support tickets grew 25 percent in two months. You have the ticket export. How would you find out why and what to do?
variants: Case prompt: tickets are rising.
intent: A case round for support, ops and product analyst roles: structure first, data second, recommendation last.
answerGuide: Clarify the facts: which tickets, what period, and what changed (new customers, release).
Segment by category, severity, customer and product area; compare to customer growth.
Look for top drivers and repeat contacts; check recent releases and documentation gaps.
Recommend actions (fix a bug, add an article, change a form) with an expected effect and how you will measure it.
followUps: What if tickets rose with customers?
What would you check first in the data?
How would you measure success?
